title: Spin-spin entanglement at high energy
authors: Michael Fucilla, Yoshitaka Hatta, Bo-Wen Xiao
abstract: Spin correlations offer a quantum-information perspective on the partonic final states produced in high-energy scattering. We discuss the spin-density matrix of a heavy quark-antiquark pair in two complementary small-$x$ processes. In coherent diffractive production, color-singlet exchange enforces an unusually strong relation between entanglement and Bell nonlocality: a longitudinal photon creates a maximally entangled pair, whereas for a transverse photon the pair is generically both entangled and Bell nonlocal, with a model-independent point of maximal entanglement. In inclusive back-to-back production, the density matrix factorizes into a hard spin tensor and the unpolarized and linearly polarized Weizsäcker--Williams gluon distributions. The latter generates an azimuthal modulation and can increase the concurrence when the dijet relative momentum and imbalance are approximately orthogonal. Strikingly, in the saturation model considered, nonlinear effects wash out this modulation for $q_\perp\lesssim 3Q_s$, whereas the dilute BFKL limit, in which $G_2/G_0\to1$, yields a maximal modulation independent of the imbalance magnitude. These results connect quantum-information observables with the Pomeron and saturation physics.
summary: This paper applies quantum information theory to study spin-spin entanglement in high-energy QCD scattering. It analyzes how entanglement manifests in different processes, such as coherent diffraction and dijet production, contrasting predictions from saturation physics against the dilute BFKL limit. The results offer novel, measurable signatures connecting quantum correlations to fundamental QCD dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates spin-spin entanglement in partonic final states produced during high-energy scattering processes in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). It aims to provide a quantum-information perspective on these complex scattering phenomena.
main_result: The entanglement properties are highly dependent on the scattering process (coherent vs. inclusive) and the kinematic regime (saturation vs. dilute limit). Specifically, longitudinal photons yield maximally entangled pairs, while the azimuthal dependence of entanglement shows a clear signature distinguishing saturation from the BFKL regime.
method: The analysis utilizes the two-qubit density matrix formalism, diagnosing entanglement via Concurrence and testing nonlocality using the CHSH inequality. Calculations are performed for specific high-energy QCD processes.
model_or_system: The physical systems are partonic final states from high-energy scattering, including coherent diffractive production and inclusive dijet production. The theoretical framework incorporates QCD evolution models like the saturation model and the BFKL (dilute) limit.
key_observables: Concurrence ($C[ho]$), Bell nonlocality (CHSH inequality violation), and the azimuthal modulation of entanglement observables.
important_parameters: The ratio of gluon distributions ($G_2/G_0$), the saturation scale ($Q_s$), and kinematic variables like $ eta$ and the azimuthal angle $\phi_{P,q}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on specific limits, such as the back-to-back dijet limit, and assumes that the partonic density matrix can be reconstructed from measured hadrons.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes the hierarchy of correlations for longitudinal vs. transverse photons in diffractive production. Figure 2 illustrates the Concurrence dependence on scattering angles, highlighting the separation between separable and Bell nonlocality domains.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes entanglement in two complementary processes: coherent diffractive production (studying the Pomeron) and inclusive back-to-back dijet production. It contrasts predictions from the saturation model with the dilute BFKL limit, focusing on the resulting azimuthal modulations.
why_interesting: While the core physics is QCD, the methodology heavily employs quantum information tools (entanglement measures, nonlocality tests) to extract physical insights, which is relevant to understanding correlations in complex quantum many-body systems.
